extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing comic-book writers and writer-artist teams
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance on generating ideas, choosing structure, pacing to page-count, scripting for artists, and preserving what is unique to comics as a medium. Targets writers (and writer/artist collaborators) producing serialized comics, graphic novels, or single-issue stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat comics as their own medium (not mere cinema or prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics should be considered in their own terms rather than being described only by cinematic or literary analogies (close-ups, long-shots, twists from films or comparisons to short stories/novels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cinema and literature supply useful vocabulary and techniques, but slavish imitation is limiting — comics that only imitate film risk being 'a film without sound nor movement'; likewise comparing long comics to novels invites unfair comparison. Instead, concentrate on areas where comics are essential and unique; consider techniques comics can do that films cannot reproduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid copying a single predecessor’s mannerisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not teach or instruct new creators to copy the generation that preceded them (e.g., 'The Marvel Way' or 'draw like John Buscema'); the industry does not need fifty people drawing or writing identically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage finding a personal approach. Imitation produces a stagnant, mechanical production; study others for pointers but develop a unique boarding/approach suited to your circumstances and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize the core idea over plot/drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'idea' (what the story is essentially about) from the drama (sequence of events). The idea is the central subject; the drama is how it unfolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the workable idea early and ensure the drama serves that idea. Example: Swamp Thing #40's idea about difficulties faced by women uses the werewolf/drama as vehicle; many comics mistake conflict-as-idea and rely on trivial 'good vs evil' resolutions via deus ex machina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source ideas from personal perception and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas germinate at the crossroads of influences and the writer’s own experiences, opinions and perceptions, not only from studying other writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a perceptive eye for trivialities in life; notice small peculiar circumstances and transform them into story seeds. Keep a 'refrigerator' of sequences/ideas until a larger idea allows insertion. Study others for pointers but rely on internal impulses for originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the material find its audience; avoid pandering to an imaginary 'reader-standard'
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t sanitize work to avoid offending a hypothetical, non-existent 'reader-standard'; instead let work find its proper level and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trying to make a work inoffensive to all results in weak, insipid stories. Rather than purging anything that might offend, consider what positively affects readers broadly (universal reactions) and trust that comics have a diverse audience beyond contrived standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use universal human reactions (humor, horror, empathy) to reach readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic human mechanisms of response are a reliable way to affect a broad readership — e.g., what makes people laugh or what truly horrifies you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze your own emotional reactions to identify raw material; jokes are often broadly effective because they 'just happen' for many listeners, and horror should be based on the writer's own deep anxieties so it reads as authentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and understand a story’s structure intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a formal structure (elliptical, parallel narratives, nonlinear anecdotal, structure-first) that best accommodates the desired effect; understand how that structure will organize the reader’s experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structures include elliptical (opening/ending echoes), simultaneous past/future fill-in while the action moves, chaptered viewpoints (each character presents part of the whole), anecdotal/nonlinear forms (Eddie Campbell-type), and structure-first experiments (e.g., telling a story via incidental television dialogue). Don’t slavishly follow steps but be conscious of the structure you choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure can lead — start with structure-first when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not always have to start with an idea;, sometimes a structural conceit or a striking sequence of pictures can be the origin of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you conceive a strong structural plan (e.g., a story told only through TV dialogue), you can fit ideas into it later. Conversely, sequences of images can be held in reserve until a larger idea makes them meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the page as a primary storytelling unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Write and plan with the page-turn in mind; use the page as the 'compass' that moves scenes without disturbing rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number pages and sketch scenes to decide how many pages each sequence will consume. Aim for pages that accomplish a meaningful unit (a beat, a mini-scene, a reveal) so that turning the page remains compelling. Use page planning to distribute information and avoid overcrowding panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan pacing, transitions, rhythm and narrative speed deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition between scenes is delicate; pacing and rhythm keep the reader 'hypnotized' and prevent them from being jolted back to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a repertoire of tools for transitions: overlapping/coincident dialogue, synchronicity of image over words, color bridges, maintaining color or motif across a cut, and positioning high-impact visuals at page-turns. Vary rhythm and flow consciously to control reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use overlapping or coincident dialogue as a practical transition tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlapping dialogue can smooth scene changes and avoid clumsy 'Meanwhile...' captions or abrupt cuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine dialogue overlap with visual continuity to create soft transitions. This is broadly applicable and less risky than some bolder experimental transitions that have only limited utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use color and shared visual motifs to bridge scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a color or strong visual motif across a cut to link scenes emotionally and visually (e.g., red blood cutting to red flowers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color can function like audio or cinematic cross-cutting to preserve mood and help the reader accept the transition without losing engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain immersion — don't 'wake' the reader unnecessarily
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful story should mesmerize: each page should lead the reader deeper until the ending delivers with impact; avoid transitions that awaken readers too soon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design openings to hook, conduction of scenes to sustain fascination, and endings that deliver catharsis. Be particularly careful with scene changes, breaks in rhythm, or piled-in exposition that will flatten involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map story beats and sequences to page counts and publication format constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the story to the concrete limits of the medium (magazine pages, issue length); plan how sequences fit into the available pages without appearing cramped or overstuffed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch a coarse page-by-page plan early, then map sequences (introductions, middle beats, climaxes, denouement) within the page budget. Prioritize strong opening pages, strong final pages, and allow space for mid-story connective material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronize parallel narratives and time their climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: When running two or more narrative lines in parallel, interlace them so their tensions and climaxes align appropriately for maximum impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which pages will carry which thread; synchronize beats so the reader experiences escalation in both strands toward the climax (example: Superman Annual — dream sequences interleaved with Fortress action so both peaks meet). Use shared images or comments for soft transitions between threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan strong opening hooks and final pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a compelling image or disorienting question to hook the reader and reserve pages for a powerful final beat that echoes the opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings that provoke 'What is this?' are useful to fish the reader; the final page should resolve emotionally and echo the opening motif or image to create cohesion and closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial resolutions dependent on deus ex machina or powers alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that resolve only because a superpower conveniently appears are usually shallow and uninteresting; don't let conflict resolution be merely an exhibition of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek resolutions that derive from the idea or character insight rather than an external convenience; ensure the central idea is meaningfully explored and the outcome feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately choose scenes and visuals; practice visual sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a notion of what is possible visually on each page: number of close-ups, angle choices, etc.; use schematic scribbles and thumbnails before scripting final copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schematic sketches help you understand what can be shown, decide camera angles (e.g., high angle for vulnerability), and avoid cramming too much information into a single page or panel. This also gives the artist a starting point and clarifies the writer’s visual intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with the artist but respect their visual intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: A good tracer/artist will likely have stronger visual instincts; supply clear intentions and schematic visual notes but don’t micromanage every visual decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give artists the necessary information (what must be read on the page, major visual beats, specific visual metaphors) and trust their craftsmanship. Over-prescription wastes the artist’s higher visual intuition. Use thumbnails and notes as communication rather than rigid instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and craft of language — avoid flat, lifeless prose
rubrics_metrics.description: The verbal element must be well-cut and alive; weak or clumsy language will undermine reader engagement even if the visuals are good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to use words to their maximum effect; sharpen dialogue and captions. Consider rhythm and the exact weight of each line; revise language to avoid bumbles and flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sequences and standalone devices in reserve for later integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Short sequences or visual tricks (e.g., Burma-Shave style billboards) can be saved until a place in a story appears where they fit organically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force a disconnected trick into a story; store promising sequences until a larger idea or emotional context allows them to contribute meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be attentive to human material — ideas arise from human thought and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The raw material of stories is human experience and emotion; explore what sensations, fears and hopes matter to you as a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, if babies starving horrifies you, interrogate why that implication disturbs you and use that emotional truth to create authentic horror or pathos. Work from what genuinely affects you to reach readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept many valid structural and narrative approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple forms of storytelling are valid (formal structures, anecdotal narratives, nonlinear explorations); don’t impose a single 'correct' form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze diverse creators (Eddie Campbell, Phil Elliott, Gabriel García Márquez borrowings) to see different organizational effects. Choose the form that best serves your idea and be willing to experiment.
